## Welcome {#home}

### Light and Health

**Learning Objectives:**

- List the qualities of good lighting for efficient, strain-free vision
- Describe the health and safety effects of poor lighting
- Explain the Daylight Factor and how it guides building design
- Distinguish direct, indirect, and semi-direct artificial lighting
- Compare filament and fluorescent lamps
- Describe biological effects of light beyond vision

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

## Qualities of Good Lighting {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Poor lighting strains the visual apparatus, causing fatigue and reduced
efficiency. Good lighting requires:

- **Sufficiency** — enough illumination to discern detail without
  strain; 15–20 foot-candles is the accepted minimum, ranging from ~5
  (stairways/corridors) to 100 (some industrial tasks)
- **Uniform distribution** — no sharp contrast across the field of work
- **Absence of glare** — excessive contrast (direct or reflected) causes
  discomfort and reduces visual acuity
- **Absence of sharp shadows** and **steadiness** — flickering causes eye
  strain and accident risk
- **Colour** — artificial light should approximate natural daylight;
  surface reflection factors matter (ceilings ~80%, walls 50–60%,
  furniture 30–40%, floors ≤15–20%)

---

## Effects of Poor Lighting {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Lighting quality is not a comfort issue alone — it has measurable
health and safety consequences, which is why the qualities above are
specified so precisely:

- **Eye strain (asthenopia)** — from insufficient illumination, glare,
  or flicker; presents as tired, aching, or watering eyes and headache
  with prolonged near work
- **Reduced visual acuity and accidents** — glare and sharp shadows
  reduce the ability to judge distance and detail, raising the risk of
  occupational and traffic accidents
- **Reduced efficiency** — both insufficient and excessive illumination
  reduce work output; there is an optimal range, not simply "more light
  is better"
- **Nystagmus** — a specific occupational eye disorder (rapid
  involuntary eye movements) historically linked to prolonged work in
  poorly lit conditions, classically described in miners

---

## Recommended Illumination Levels {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Required illumination varies by the precision of the task — a single
"sufficient" threshold does not apply everywhere:

| Setting/task | Approximate illumination (foot-candles) |
|---|---|
| Stairways, corridors, storage | ~5 |
| General living/working areas | 15–20 (accepted minimum) |
| Reading, classrooms, offices | 20–30 |
| Fine assembly, precision industrial work | up to 100 |

**Why this table matters:** it operationalizes "sufficiency" from the
previous slide — a corridor and an operating table are not held to the
same lighting standard, because the visual precision each task demands
is different.

---

## Natural Lighting and the Daylight Factor {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Effective natural lighting depends on building **orientation** (north/
south preferred in the tropics to avoid direct east/west sun heating
rooms), **window design** (tall windows → deeper penetration; broad
windows → wider diffusion), and **interior colour scheme** (white
ceiling, light-tinted upper walls, darker lower walls for comfortable
contrast).

Because daylight intensity constantly changes, it's measured relative to
outdoor conditions using the **Daylight Factor (DF)**:

`DF = (Indoor illumination / Simultaneous outdoor illumination) × 100`

Recommended minimum: **8% in living rooms, 10% in kitchens**.

---

## Artificial Lighting {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

| Type | Light distribution |
|---|---|
| **Direct** | 90–100% projected straight down; efficient but casts sharp shadows |
| **Semi-direct** | 60–90% down, rest reflected off ceiling |
| **Indirect** | 90–100% projected up to ceiling/walls; general room illumination without object-specific light |
| **Semi-indirect** | 60–90% up, rest down |

**Lamp types:** filament lamps (heat a tungsten filament; efficiency
drops 30–40% with dust accumulation on the bulb) vs. **fluorescent
lamps** (more efficient, cooler, light output closer to natural
daylight — mercury vapour tube with fluorescent coating converting UV to
visible light).

---

## Biological Effects of Light {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

Light's effects on the body extend well beyond vision:

- **Phototherapy** — daylight/blue light degrades bilirubin, used
  therapeutically for **neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia** in premature
  infants
- **Circadian effects** — influences biologic rhythms of body
  temperature and physical activity
- Stimulates **melanin synthesis** and activates **vitamin D precursors**
  in skin
- Affects adrenocortical secretion and food consumption patterns

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 1

The Daylight Factor is best described as:

- The absolute illumination measured in foot-candles
- [The ratio of indoor illumination to simultaneous outdoor illumination, expressed as a percentage]{.correct data-explanation="DF = (indoor illumination / simultaneous outdoor illumination) x 100 — used instead of an absolute foot-candle measure because outdoor daylight intensity constantly changes."}
- The number of windows per room
- The colour temperature of daylight
:::

## Self-Check: Question 2 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 2

Which artificial lighting type projects 90–100% of light upward toward
the ceiling and walls, giving general room illumination rather than
object-specific light?

- Direct lighting
- Semi-direct lighting
- [Indirect lighting]{.correct data-explanation="Indirect lighting projects 90-100% of light upward to be reflected off the ceiling and walls, producing diffuse general illumination without directly lighting any specific object."}
- Semi-indirect lighting
:::

### Question 4
